Anji Wu Changshuo.　　This set of couplets in stone and drum was written in the sixth year of the Republic of China (1917), when Wu Changshuo was 74 years old. The brushwork is thick and fluent, both round and square, and rich in variation, full of ancient and concise, sober and unrestrained jinshui, which is a fine stone drum script created by Wu Changshuo in his later years.　　The stone drums were carved in the Qin Dynasty during the Warring States period and were named after their resemblance to drums, and were also called hunting stones because of the inscriptions describing noblemen's hunting trips. There are ten stone drums, each inscribed with an ancient song of the pre-Qin Dynasty. It is unique among ancient calligraphic texts in terms of its grand and dignified physique, majestic and rounded brushwork. Due to its age, the handwriting has been worn out. The stone drum is now in the National Palace Museum in Beijing (note: the location of the exhibition is subject to change). 　　As another master of seal script after Deng Shiru, Wu Changshuo expanded the field of Deng Shiru's exploration based on the small seal script to the Great Seal Script of the Shang and Zhou Dynasties, mainly focusing on the Shigu script. He broke the ancient concept of the Qing dynasty of chasing gold with the brush, and used a natural and spacious running brush to enter the seal script, expressing the aesthetic interest of the majestic and pale characters of the three dynasties in terms of both the form and the spirit, and injecting a new atmosphere into the ancient method of the Great Seal Script.
